sectionTitle: Identification of ions by chemical and spectroscopic means (chemistry only)

specStatements.text: Flame tests can be used to identify some metal ions (cations). Lithium, sodium, potassium, calcium and copper compounds produce distinctive colours in flame tests:
lithium compounds result in a crimson flame
sodium compounds result in a yellow flame
potassium compounds result in a lilac flame
calcium compounds result in an orange-red flame
copper compounds result in a green flame.
If a sample containing a mixture of ions is used some flame colours can be masked.
Students should be able to identify species from the results of the tests in 4.8.3.1 to 4.8.3.5.
Flame colours of other metal ions are not required knowledge.
Sodium hydroxide solution can be used to identify some metal ions (cations).

Solutions of aluminium, calcium and magnesium ions form white precipitates when sodium hydroxide solution is added but only the aluminium hydroxide precipitate dissolves in excess sodium hydroxide solution.
Solutions of copper(II), iron(II) and iron(III) ions form coloured precipitates when sodium hydroxide solution is added.
Copper(II) forms a blue precipitate, iron(II) a green precipitate and iron(III) a brown precipitate.
Students should be able to write balanced equations for the reactions to produce the insoluble hydroxides.
Students are not expected to write equations for the production of sodium aluminate.
Carbonates react with dilute acids to form carbon dioxide gas. Carbon dioxide can be identified with limewater.
Halide ions in solution produce precipitates with silver nitrate solution in the presence of dilute nitric acid. Silver chloride is white, silver bromide is cream and silver iodide is yellow.
Sulfate ions in solution produce a white precipitate with barium chloride solution in the presence of dilute hydrochloric acid.
Required practical 7: use of chemical tests to identify the ions in unknown single ionic compounds covering the ions from sections Flame tests to Sulfates .
Elements and compounds can be detected and identified using instrumental methods. Instrumental methods are accurate, sensitive and rapid.
Students should be able to state advantages of instrumental methods compared with the chemical tests in this specification.
Flame emission spectroscopy is an example of an instrumental method used to analyse metal ions in solutions.

The sample is put into a flame and the light given out is passed through a spectroscope. The output is a line spectrum that can be analysed to identify the metal ions in the solution and measure their concentrations.

Students should be able to interpret an instrumental result given appropriate data in chart or tabular form, when accompanied by a reference set in the same form, limited to flame emission spectroscopy.

scopeNotes.statement: Flame colours of other metal ions are not required knowledge.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Only the five flame colours named in the specification are taught and assessed: lithium crimson, sodium yellow, potassium lilac, calcium orange-red and copper green. Where other metals appear in this content (aluminium, magnesium, iron(II), iron(III)), they are identified only by their reactions with sodium hydroxide solution, and no flame colour is stated, implied or required for them. No question asks for, or can be answered by, a flame colour outside the five named ions.

scopeNotes.statement: Students are not expected to write equations for the production of sodium aluminate.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Equation writing is confined to the formation of the insoluble hydroxides, as required by 4.8.3.2. The dissolving of the aluminium hydroxide precipitate in excess sodium hydroxide solution is treated purely as an observation used to distinguish aluminium from calcium and magnesium; no product of that dissolving is named and no equation for it is written or asked for anywhere in this content.

concepts.definition: A test in which a sample of a compound is held in a Bunsen flame; some metal ions give the flame a distinctive colour, which identifies the metal ion present.
A positively charged ion. Flame tests and sodium hydroxide solution are used to identify metal ions, which are cations.
The distinctive flame colour produced by lithium compounds.
The distinctive flame colour produced by sodium compounds.
The distinctive flame colour produced by potassium compounds.
The distinctive flame colour produced by calcium compounds.
The distinctive flame colour produced by copper compounds.
If a sample contains a mixture of ions, one flame colour can hide another. A strong colour such as the yellow of sodium can mask a weaker colour, so an ion that is present may not be seen.

Sodium hydroxide solution is added to a solution of the unknown compound. Metal ions that form insoluble hydroxides give a precipitate whose colour, and behaviour in excess sodium hydroxide, identifies the metal ion.
Solutions of aluminium, calcium and magnesium ions all form white precipitates when sodium hydroxide solution is added, so the colour alone does not identify which of the three is present.
Of the three white precipitates, only the aluminium hydroxide precipitate dissolves when excess sodium hydroxide solution is added. This distinguishes aluminium ions from calcium and magnesium ions.
Solutions of copper(II), iron(II) and iron(III) ions form coloured precipitates when sodium hydroxide solution is added, and the colour identifies the ion.
The precipitate formed by copper(II) ions with sodium hydroxide solution.
The precipitate formed by iron(II) ions with sodium hydroxide solution.
The precipitate formed by iron(III) ions with sodium hydroxide solution.
An equation showing only the ions that form the insoluble hydroxide, balanced for both atoms and charge, for example Fe3+(aq) + 3OH-(aq) → Fe(OH)3(s) and Cu2+(aq) + 2OH-(aq) → Cu(OH)2(s).
A full balanced equation for the reaction of a soluble salt with sodium hydroxide, for example CuSO4 + 2NaOH → Cu(OH)2 + Na2SO4 and FeCl3 + 3NaOH → Fe(OH)3 + 3NaCl.
Carbonates react with dilute acids to form carbon dioxide gas, seen as fizzing. The gas must then be identified to confirm that a carbonate is present.
Carbon dioxide is identified by bubbling the gas through limewater, which turns milky (cloudy) because insoluble calcium carbonate is formed.

concepts.term: Silver nitrate test for halide ions
concepts.definition: Halide ions in solution produce precipitates with silver nitrate solution in the presence of dilute nitric acid. Nitric acid is used because it adds no halide ions of its own.
Silver chloride is white, silver bromide is cream and silver iodide is yellow, so the colour of the precipitate identifies which halide ion is present.

concepts.term: Barium chloride test for sulfate ions
concepts.definition: Sulfate ions in solution produce a white precipitate with barium chloride solution in the presence of dilute hydrochloric acid.

Use of chemical tests to identify the ions in unknown single ionic compounds, covering the ions from flame tests through to sulfates. Both the positive and the negative ion must be identified before a compound can be named.
A method that uses a machine to detect and identify elements and compounds, rather than a chemical test carried out by hand.
The three properties the specification gives for instrumental methods: they give results close to the true value, they can detect very small amounts of a substance, and they give results quickly.

Compared with the chemical tests in this specification, instrumental methods are more accurate, can detect much smaller amounts of a substance, and work far more quickly, including on samples containing mixtures of ions.
An instrumental method used to analyse metal ions in solutions.
The instrument through which the light given out by the sample in the flame is passed, producing the spectrum that is analysed.
The output of flame emission spectroscopy: a pattern of separate lines that can be analysed to identify the metal ions in the solution and measure their concentrations.

concepts.term: Measuring concentration by flame emission spectroscopy
concepts.definition: As well as identifying which metal ions are present, the line spectrum can be analysed to measure the concentration of those ions in the solution.
A set of results for known metal ions, given in the same chart or tabular form as the sample result, against which the sample's line spectrum is compared in order to identify the metal ions present.

misconceptions.question: What colour flame do sodium compounds give?
misconceptions.correct: Sodium compounds result in a yellow flame.
misconceptions.misconception: Sodium gives an orange flame - street lights are orange and they contain sodium.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Sodium street lamps and burning sodium in a hot flame both look orange to the eye, and the yellow of sodium sits next to the orange-red of calcium in the list, so the two blur together.
misconceptions.correction: The specification is precise: sodium compounds result in a yellow flame, and calcium compounds result in an orange-red flame. These are two different colours belonging to two different ions.

misconceptions.question: Which of lithium and potassium gives the crimson flame?
misconceptions.correct: Lithium compounds result in a crimson flame; potassium compounds result in a lilac flame.
misconceptions.misconception: Lithium is the lilac one and potassium is the crimson one.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Both are Group 1 metals learned in the same list, and neither colour is an everyday word, so the pairing is memorised as a bare fact and is easily swapped.
misconceptions.correction: Lithium gives crimson (a deep red) and potassium gives lilac (a pale purple). The two must be attached to the right metal, because in an identification question the colour is the only evidence for the cation.

misconceptions.question: What colour flame do copper compounds give?
misconceptions.correct: Copper compounds result in a green flame.
misconceptions.misconception: Copper gives a blue flame, because copper compounds and copper solutions are blue.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Copper(II) sulfate solution is blue and copper(II) hydroxide is a blue precipitate, so the colour blue becomes attached to copper generally and is carried over into the flame test.
misconceptions.correction: The colour of a compound and the colour it gives a flame are separate facts. Copper compounds result in a green flame, even though many of them are blue in solution and give a blue precipitate with sodium hydroxide.

misconceptions.question: What is seen when a sample containing a mixture of metal ions is flame tested?
misconceptions.correct: Some flame colours can be masked, so an ion that is present may give no visible colour.
misconceptions.misconception: You will see all the colours at once, so a mixture just shows every ion that is there.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students expect a test to be additive - if two ions are present, two colours should appear - and mixing coloured paints or lights is the everyday model they reach for.
misconceptions.correction: If a sample containing a mixture of ions is used, some flame colours can be masked. A strong colour hides a weaker one, so a negative flame test does not prove an ion is absent.

misconceptions.question: Which ion does a flame test identify?
misconceptions.correct: A flame test identifies some metal ions, which are cations.
misconceptions.misconception: The flame colour tells you the negative ion, so a chloride would have its own flame colour.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Compound names put the non-metal part last and it is the part students often focus on, and the tests for halides and sulfates are learned alongside flame tests, so the two get mixed.
misconceptions.correction: Flame tests identify metal ions (cations) only. Negative ions are identified separately - carbonates with dilute acid and limewater, halides with silver nitrate, sulfates with barium chloride.

misconceptions.question: Do sodium chloride and sodium sulfate give the same flame colour?
misconceptions.correct: Yes - both give a yellow flame, because the colour comes from the sodium ion.
misconceptions.misconception: The flame colour belongs to the whole compound, so different sodium compounds give different colours.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students think in terms of substances rather than ions, so the test feels like a test on the compound rather than on one ion inside it.
misconceptions.correction: The colour comes from the metal ion. Every sodium compound gives a yellow flame, which is why the flame test names the cation but leaves the rest of the compound unknown.

misconceptions.question: How are the aluminium, calcium and magnesium precipitates told apart?
misconceptions.correct: By adding excess sodium hydroxide solution - only the aluminium hydroxide precipitate dissolves.
misconceptions.misconception: You can tell them apart by looking - the three whites are slightly different shades.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Every other precipitate in this topic is identified by its colour, so students expect colour to do the work here too.
misconceptions.correction: All three are simply white. Colour gives no information, so a second step is required: excess sodium hydroxide solution dissolves only the aluminium hydroxide precipitate. A flame test can then separate calcium from magnesium.

misconceptions.question: What happens to the white precipitates when excess sodium hydroxide solution is added?
misconceptions.correct: Only the aluminium hydroxide precipitate dissolves; the calcium and magnesium precipitates remain.
misconceptions.misconception: Add enough sodium hydroxide and any white precipitate will dissolve again.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students generalise from the aluminium result, and from everyday experience that adding more solvent eventually dissolves a solid.
misconceptions.correction: The specification is exact: only the aluminium hydroxide precipitate dissolves in excess sodium hydroxide solution. This is precisely why the excess step is a useful test - if the precipitate stays, aluminium is not present.

misconceptions.question: Which iron ion gives the brown precipitate with sodium hydroxide solution?
misconceptions.correct: Iron(III) gives a brown precipitate; iron(II) gives a green precipitate.
misconceptions.misconception: Iron(II) is the brown one and iron(III) is the green one.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The two iron ions differ only by a Roman numeral, and the pair of colours is memorised without any hook to fix which goes with which.
misconceptions.correction: Iron(II) gives green and iron(III) gives brown. Rust is iron(III) and is brown, which is a reliable way to fix the higher charge to the brown precipitate.

misconceptions.question: What colour precipitate does copper(II) give with sodium hydroxide solution?
misconceptions.correct: Copper(II) forms a blue precipitate.
misconceptions.misconception: Copper gives a green precipitate, because copper is the green one.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Copper compounds give a green flame, so green becomes the colour attached to copper, and it is then carried into the precipitate test as well.
misconceptions.correction: Copper is green in a flame test but blue as a hydroxide precipitate. Green precipitate means iron(II), not copper.

misconceptions.question: Is Fe3+(aq) + OH-(aq) → Fe(OH)3(s) an acceptable ionic equation?
misconceptions.correct: No. The equation must be Fe3+(aq) + 3OH-(aq) → Fe(OH)3(s), which balances both atoms and charge.
misconceptions.misconception: As long as the formulas are right, one of each ion is enough - the equation shows what reacts with what.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students read an ionic equation as a statement of which ions are involved rather than as a quantitative balance, and charge balancing is often not checked at all.
misconceptions.correction: A balanced equation must have the same number of each type of atom and the same total charge on both sides. Three OH- ions are needed for each Fe3+ ion: +3 and -3 give a neutral solid.

misconceptions.question: What is the formula of the hydroxide formed by iron(III) ions?
misconceptions.correct: Fe(OH)3, because the 3+ charge on the iron ion requires three hydroxide ions.
misconceptions.misconception: Metal hydroxides are all written the same way, so iron hydroxide is Fe(OH)2.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The 2+ ions met most often (magnesium, calcium, copper(II)) all give M(OH)2, so that pattern is copied without checking the charge on the metal ion.
misconceptions.correction: The subscript follows the charge on the metal ion: Mg(OH)2 and Cu(OH)2 from 2+ ions, but Al(OH)3 and Fe(OH)3 from 3+ ions. Get the formula right before balancing.

misconceptions.question: A solid fizzes with dilute acid. Is it a carbonate?
misconceptions.correct: Not proven. The gas must be shown to be carbon dioxide by bubbling it through limewater.
misconceptions.misconception: Fizzing with acid is the carbonate test, so bubbles are enough to prove it.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Fizzing is the memorable part of the demonstration, and it happens immediately, so it feels like the result rather than the first half of the test.
misconceptions.correction: Carbonates react with dilute acids to form carbon dioxide gas, but other reactions also produce gas. The identification is completed by the limewater test, which turns milky with carbon dioxide.

misconceptions.question: Which gas do carbonates give with dilute acid?
misconceptions.correct: Carbon dioxide.
misconceptions.misconception: Acids give off hydrogen, so a carbonate and acid must give hydrogen too.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Metal plus acid producing hydrogen is met earlier and more often, and both reactions look the same - a solid fizzing in acid.
misconceptions.correction: Metals with dilute acid give hydrogen; carbonates with dilute acid give carbon dioxide. Hydrogen pops with a lighted splint, whereas carbon dioxide turns limewater milky.

misconceptions.question: Why does limewater turn milky?
misconceptions.correct: Because insoluble calcium carbonate is formed, and the fine solid makes the solution cloudy.
misconceptions.misconception: The carbon dioxide dissolves in the limewater and that is what clouds it.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The gas visibly disappears into the liquid, so dissolving is the obvious explanation, and students do not expect a gas to take part in a precipitation reaction.
misconceptions.correction: The cloudiness is a precipitate. Carbon dioxide reacts with the calcium hydroxide in limewater to form insoluble calcium carbonate, which is the white solid suspended in the liquid.

misconceptions.question: Which acid is used with silver nitrate solution in the halide test?
misconceptions.correct: Dilute nitric acid.
misconceptions.misconception: Dilute hydrochloric acid - it is the acid we normally use in tests.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Hydrochloric acid is the default acid in the laboratory and is used in the sulfate test on the very next page, so it gets applied here too.
misconceptions.correction: Hydrochloric acid contains chloride ions, which would themselves give a white precipitate of silver chloride and a false positive. Dilute nitric acid is used because it adds no halide ions.

misconceptions.question: What colour is silver bromide?
misconceptions.correct: Cream. Silver iodide is yellow.
misconceptions.misconception: Silver bromide is yellow and silver iodide is cream.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Cream and yellow are close colours and the two halides are learned as a pair, so the labels are easily attached the wrong way round.
misconceptions.correction: The colours deepen down the group: silver chloride white, silver bromide cream, silver iodide yellow. Keeping them in group order fixes which is which.

misconceptions.question: Which acid is used with barium chloride solution in the sulfate test?
misconceptions.correct: Dilute hydrochloric acid.
misconceptions.misconception: Dilute sulfuric acid - we are testing for sulfates, so sulfuric acid fits.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The name of the acid matches the name of the ion being tested for, which feels like a helpful pairing rather than a fatal one.
misconceptions.correction: Sulfuric acid contains sulfate ions, so it would produce a white precipitate of barium sulfate with every sample. Dilute hydrochloric acid is used because it adds no sulfate ions.

misconceptions.question: A solution gives a white precipitate. Does it contain sulfate ions?
misconceptions.correct: Only if the white precipitate is formed with barium chloride solution and dilute hydrochloric acid.
misconceptions.misconception: A white precipitate means a sulfate, because barium sulfate is the white one.
misconceptions.whyItArises: White precipitates appear in more than one test in this topic, but the sulfate test is the one where white is the whole result, so white becomes shorthand for sulfate.
misconceptions.correction: The reagent matters as much as the colour. White with barium chloride and hydrochloric acid indicates sulfate ions; white with sodium hydroxide indicates aluminium, calcium or magnesium; white with silver nitrate and nitric acid indicates chloride.

misconceptions.question: Is one positive test enough to name an unknown ionic compound?
misconceptions.correct: No. Both the positive ion and the negative ion must be identified.
misconceptions.misconception: Once a test comes out positive you know what the compound is, so you can stop there.
misconceptions.whyItArises: In practical work the first positive result is a satisfying moment, and the tests are learned individually rather than as a sequence that has to be completed.
misconceptions.correction: Required practical 7 identifies the ions in unknown single ionic compounds, and a compound has two parts. A yellow flame tells you the cation is sodium but leaves the anion completely unknown.

misconceptions.question: What is an advantage of instrumental methods over the chemical tests in this specification?
misconceptions.correct: They are accurate, sensitive and rapid - in particular they detect very small amounts.
misconceptions.misconception: They are cheaper and simpler, because a machine does the work for you.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Automation is associated with saving money and effort in everyday life, so students transfer that assumption to laboratory instruments.
misconceptions.correction: The advantages the specification gives are accuracy, sensitivity and speed. Instruments are in fact expensive and need trained operators - cost and ease of use are not among their advantages.

misconceptions.question: What can a flame emission line spectrum tell you?
misconceptions.correct: Which metal ions are present in the solution and what their concentrations are.
misconceptions.misconception: It only tells you which metals are there - you would need a different method to find how much.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The method grows out of the flame test, which is purely qualitative, so students assume the instrumental version is a better version of the same qualitative result.
misconceptions.correction: The specification states that the line spectrum can be analysed both to identify the metal ions in the solution and to measure their concentrations.

misconceptions.question: What does the output of the spectroscope look like?
misconceptions.correct: A line spectrum - a set of separate lines.
misconceptions.misconception: A rainbow, because a spectroscope splits light into a continuous spread of colours.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The word spectrum is met first with the continuous spectrum of white light through a prism, and that image is the one students already hold.
misconceptions.correction: The output is a line spectrum. Each metal gives its own particular set of lines, and it is that pattern of lines, not a continuous band of colour, that identifies the metal.

misconceptions.question: A sample spectrum contains all the lines of one reference metal plus some extra lines. What does that mean?
misconceptions.correct: That metal is present, and at least one other metal is present as well.
misconceptions.misconception: The spectra do not match exactly, so that metal is not present.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students treat matching as all-or-nothing, as in matching fingerprints, and do not expect a real sample to be a mixture whose spectra overlay each other.
misconceptions.correction: A solution may contain several metal ions, and the sample spectrum is then all their line patterns together. If every line of a reference set appears in the sample, that metal is present; extra lines point to further metals.

misconceptions.question: Which is more accurate, a chemical test or an instrumental method?
misconceptions.correct: The instrumental method - the specification states instrumental methods are accurate, sensitive and rapid.
misconceptions.misconception: Chemical tests are more trustworthy because you see the result with your own eyes.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Direct observation feels like better evidence than a reading from a machine, and students have carried out the chemical tests themselves but not the instrumental one.
misconceptions.correction: Judging cream against yellow by eye, or missing a masked flame colour, makes chemical tests far less reliable. Instrumental methods are accurate, sensitive and rapid, which is why analytical laboratories use them.

misconceptions.question: Can lithium and calcium be told apart by a flame test?
misconceptions.correct: Yes - lithium gives a crimson flame and calcium gives an orange-red flame.
misconceptions.misconception: Crimson and orange-red are both just red, so a red flame could be either.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Both colours are described with red words, and in a photograph or a rushed demonstration they can look similar, so students merge them into a single category.
misconceptions.correction: The specification names them separately: lithium crimson, calcium orange-red. Crimson is a deep red; the calcium flame is distinctly more orange. If a question gives one of these words, it is naming one specific ion.

misconceptions.question: Do sodium and potassium give the same flame colour?
misconceptions.correct: No - sodium gives yellow and potassium gives lilac.
misconceptions.misconception: They are both Group 1 metals right next to each other, so their flame colours must be much the same.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Group 1 is taught as a family with very similar chemical properties, so students expect similar behaviour in a flame test too.
misconceptions.correction: Flame colours do not follow group trends. Every one of the five named metals has its own distinct colour, which is exactly what makes the flame test useful for telling them apart.

misconceptions.question: What colour is the iron(II) hydroxide precipitate?
misconceptions.correct: Green.
misconceptions.misconception: Iron(II) solutions look almost colourless, so the precipitate must be white.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Iron(II) solutions are only pale green, so in a test tube they can look colourless, and students then expect a colourless precipitate.
misconceptions.correction: Iron(II) forms a green precipitate with sodium hydroxide solution. White precipitates in this topic come from aluminium, calcium and magnesium, not from iron.

misconceptions.question: Is CuSO4 + 2NaOH → Cu(OH)2 + 2NaSO4 balanced?
misconceptions.correct: No. NaSO4 is not a correct formula; the equation is CuSO4 + 2NaOH → Cu(OH)2 + Na2SO4.
misconceptions.misconception: Balancing is about putting the right big numbers in front, so a 2 in front of the sodium sulfate fixes the sodium.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Balancing is practised as an arithmetic exercise on coefficients, so students adjust the numbers in front without checking that each formula is itself correct.
misconceptions.correction: Formulas are fixed by the charges on the ions and must be written correctly first. Sodium sulfate is Na2SO4; only then are coefficients chosen to balance the equation.

misconceptions.question: What is limewater?
misconceptions.correct: A solution of calcium hydroxide, used to identify carbon dioxide.
misconceptions.misconception: Limewater is sodium hydroxide solution - the alkali we use everywhere else in this topic.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Sodium hydroxide solution is the reagent used in the cation tests immediately before, so it becomes the default alkali in the student's mind.
misconceptions.correction: Limewater is calcium hydroxide solution. That is why carbon dioxide turns it milky - the precipitate formed is calcium carbonate.

misconceptions.question: Are all the silver halide precipitates white?
misconceptions.correct: No - silver chloride is white, silver bromide is cream and silver iodide is yellow.
misconceptions.misconception: Precipitates with silver nitrate are white, so any halide gives a white solid.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Silver chloride is usually the example demonstrated first and is genuinely white, so it becomes the model for the whole test.
misconceptions.correction: The three colours are the point of the test - they are what identifies which halide ion is present. Reporting them all as white throws away the information.

misconceptions.question: Why is dilute acid added in the silver nitrate and barium chloride tests?
misconceptions.correct: To remove ions that would otherwise give a false positive result.
misconceptions.misconception: The acid brings out the colour of the precipitate so it is easier to see.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The acid has no visible effect of its own, so students invent a purpose for it, and colour is the feature they are attending to in these tests.
misconceptions.correction: The acid is chosen so that it does not add the ion being tested for: nitric acid in the halide test adds no halide ions, and hydrochloric acid in the sulfate test adds no sulfate ions. It plays no part in the colour.

misconceptions.question: How does flame emission spectroscopy differ from a flame test?
misconceptions.correct: The light given out is passed through a spectroscope and a line spectrum is produced and analysed.
misconceptions.misconception: It is just a flame test done carefully - you look at the flame colour and match it against a chart.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Both methods put a sample into a flame, and the word flame in the name suggests the same, purely visual, procedure.
misconceptions.correction: In flame emission spectroscopy the light is analysed by an instrument, not by eye. The line spectrum identifies the metal ions even in a mixture, and measures their concentrations, neither of which a flame test can do.

misconceptions.question: Where does the light analysed in flame emission spectroscopy come from?
misconceptions.correct: The sample is put into a flame and the light given out by it is passed through a spectroscope.
misconceptions.misconception: A beam of light is shone through the sample and the instrument measures what gets through.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Colorimetry and other absorption methods work that way, and students expect an analytical instrument to shine something at a sample.
misconceptions.correction: This method uses emission: the sample itself gives out light when it is put into the flame, and that emitted light is passed through the spectroscope.

mcqs.stem: A student carries out a flame test on a solid ionic compound. What does the colour of the flame identify?

options.text: the metal ion (cation) present in the compound
options.rationale: Flame tests can be used to identify some metal ions (cations); the colour comes from the metal ion.

options.text: the non-metal ion (anion) present in the compound
options.rationale: Students who focus on the second half of the compound's name expect the flame colour to name the negative ion.

options.text: the compound as a whole, not any single ion
options.rationale: Thinking in substances rather than ions, students treat the test as a test on the compound.

options.text: the temperature reached by the Bunsen flame
options.rationale: Flame colour is associated with heat in everyday life, so temperature is a tempting reading of the observation.

mcqs.stem: A compound produces a crimson flame in a flame test. Which ion does it contain?

options.text: potassium ions, K+
options.rationale: Students who have swapped the two Group 1 colours give potassium the crimson flame.

options.text: lithium ions, Li+
options.rationale: Lithium compounds result in a crimson flame.

options.text: calcium ions, Ca2+
options.rationale: Crimson and orange-red are both red words, so calcium is chosen by students who merge the two.

options.text: sodium ions, Na+
options.rationale: Sodium is the most familiar flame test, so it is picked when the exact colour is not recalled.

mcqs.stem: A potassium compound and a lithium compound are each tested in a flame. Which pair of colours is correct?

options.text: potassium crimson, lithium lilac
options.rationale: This is the exact swap students make when the two Group 1 colours are memorised without a hook.

options.text: potassium lilac, lithium orange-red
options.rationale: Students who treat crimson and orange-red as the same red will accept orange-red for lithium.

options.text: potassium lilac, lithium crimson
options.rationale: Potassium compounds result in a lilac flame and lithium compounds result in a crimson flame.

options.text: potassium yellow, lithium crimson
options.rationale: Expecting Group 1 metals to behave alike, students give potassium the sodium colour.

mcqs.stem: A white solid gives an orange-red flame. Its solution gives a white precipitate with sodium hydroxide solution which does not dissolve in excess. Which ion is present?

options.text: lithium ions, Li+
options.rationale: Students who cannot separate crimson from orange-red read the flame colour as lithium.

options.text: aluminium ions, Al3+
options.rationale: Students who think every white precipitate dissolves in excess ignore the second clue and pick aluminium.

options.text: magnesium ions, Mg2+
options.rationale: Magnesium fits the precipitate evidence, but it is not one of the five ions with a required flame colour.

options.text: calcium ions, Ca2+
options.rationale: Calcium gives an orange-red flame and a white hydroxide precipitate that does not dissolve in excess sodium hydroxide.

mcqs.stem: A copper compound and a calcium compound are each held in a Bunsen flame. Which colours are seen?

options.text: copper green, calcium orange-red
options.rationale: Copper compounds result in a green flame and calcium compounds result in an orange-red flame.

options.text: copper blue, calcium orange-red
options.rationale: Blue copper(II) solutions and the blue hydroxide precipitate lead students to expect a blue flame.

options.text: copper blue-green, calcium crimson
options.rationale: Combines the blue-copper error with treating crimson and orange-red as interchangeable.

options.text: copper green, calcium yellow
options.rationale: Students who muddle the yellow of sodium with the orange-red of calcium choose yellow here.

mcqs.stem: A solid contains both sodium ions and potassium ions. The flame test shows only a yellow flame. What is the best explanation?

options.text: the two flame colours mix, and the mixture produced is yellow
options.rationale: Students apply a paint-mixing model, expecting the colours to combine rather than one to hide the other.

options.text: the strong sodium colour masks the lilac potassium colour
options.rationale: If a sample containing a mixture of ions is used, some flame colours can be masked.

options.text: potassium also gives a yellow flame, so both ions are shown
options.rationale: Expecting Group 1 metals to behave alike, students assume potassium shares sodium's colour.

options.text: the potassium compound decomposed before reaching the flame
options.rationale: Invoking decomposition is a common way to explain away an ion that fails to show up.

mcqs.stem: Three solutions each give a white precipitate with sodium hydroxide solution. Which step identifies the aluminium one?

options.text: compare the shades of white of the three precipitates formed
options.rationale: Because every other precipitate here is identified by colour, students expect colour to work again.

options.text: add excess sodium hydroxide; the calcium precipitate dissolves
options.rationale: Students who think excess alkali dissolves any hydroxide attach the behaviour to the wrong ion.

options.text: add excess sodium hydroxide; only this precipitate dissolves
options.rationale: Only the aluminium hydroxide precipitate dissolves in excess sodium hydroxide solution.

options.text: warm the mixture; only the aluminium precipitate turns brown
options.rationale: Heating is a plausible-sounding extra step, and brown is remembered from the iron(III) precipitate.

mcqs.stem: Sodium hydroxide solution is added to magnesium chloride solution until it is in excess. What is observed?

options.text: a white precipitate forms and dissolves when excess is added
options.rationale: Students generalise the aluminium behaviour to every white hydroxide precipitate.

options.text: a white precipitate forms, showing sulfate ions are present
options.rationale: White precipitate has become shorthand for sulfate, regardless of which reagent was added.

options.text: no precipitate forms because magnesium salts are all soluble
options.rationale: Confusing the solubility of magnesium chloride with that of magnesium hydroxide is a common slip.

options.text: a white precipitate forms and stays when excess is added
options.rationale: Magnesium ions form a white precipitate, and only the aluminium hydroxide precipitate dissolves in excess.

mcqs.stem: Sodium hydroxide solution is added to separate solutions of an iron(II) salt and an iron(III) salt. Which precipitate colours form?

options.text: iron(II) green, iron(III) brown
options.rationale: Iron(II) forms a green precipitate and iron(III) a brown precipitate.

options.text: iron(II) brown, iron(III) green
options.rationale: The two iron ions differ only by a Roman numeral, so the colours are easily swapped.

options.text: iron(II) white, iron(III) brown
options.rationale: Iron(II) solutions look almost colourless, so students expect a white precipitate.

options.text: iron(II) brown, iron(III) brown
options.rationale: Rust is brown, so students assign brown to iron in general rather than to iron(III) only.

mcqs.stem: A pale green solution forms a green precipitate when sodium hydroxide solution is added. Which ion is present?

options.text: copper(II) ions, Cu2+
options.rationale: The green flame colour of copper leads students to expect a green copper precipitate.

options.text: iron(II) ions, Fe2+
options.rationale: Iron(II) forms a green precipitate with sodium hydroxide solution.

options.text: iron(III) ions, Fe3+
options.rationale: Students who have swapped the iron colours read green as iron(III).

options.text: magnesium ions, Mg2+
options.rationale: Magnesium is chosen by students who know only that it forms a precipitate with sodium hydroxide.

mcqs.stem: Which ionic equation correctly shows the precipitate formed when sodium hydroxide solution is added to iron(III) chloride solution?

options.text: Fe3+(aq) + OH-(aq) → Fe(OH)3(s)
options.rationale: Students who read the equation as a list of reacting ions do not check that the charges balance.

options.text: Fe3+(aq) + 2OH-(aq) → Fe(OH)2(s)
options.rationale: The M(OH)2 pattern from magnesium and copper(II) is copied without checking the iron(III) charge.

options.text: Fe3+(aq) + 3OH-(aq) → Fe(OH)3(s)
options.rationale: Atoms and charge both balance, and the insoluble hydroxide is correctly shown as a solid.

options.text: Fe3+(aq) + 3OH-(aq) → Fe(OH)3(aq)
options.rationale: State symbols are added last and carelessly, so the precipitate is left labelled as a solution.

mcqs.stem: Copper(II) sulfate solution reacts with sodium hydroxide solution to form a precipitate. Which balanced equation is correct?

options.text: CuSO4 + NaOH → Cu(OH)2 + Na2SO4
options.rationale: Students who treat the equation as a statement of what reacts leave the sodium and hydrogen unbalanced.

options.text: CuSO4 + 2NaOH → Cu(OH)2 + 2NaSO4
options.rationale: Balancing by adjusting coefficients only, without checking that NaSO4 is a valid formula.

options.text: CuSO4 + 2NaOH → CuO + Na2SO4 + H2O
options.rationale: This balances perfectly, so students who check only the atom counts and not the products accept it.

options.text: CuSO4 + 2NaOH → Cu(OH)2 + Na2SO4
options.rationale: The formulas are correct and every element balances, giving the insoluble copper(II) hydroxide.

mcqs.stem: Which statement about carbonates and the test for them is correct?

options.text: carbonates react with dilute acids to form carbon dioxide
options.rationale: This is exactly what the specification states for the reaction of carbonates with dilute acids.

options.text: carbonates react with dilute acids to form hydrogen gas
options.rationale: Metal plus acid giving hydrogen is met earlier and looks identical in the test tube.

options.text: carbonates are identified using sodium hydroxide solution
options.rationale: Sodium hydroxide is the default alkali in this topic, so it is substituted for limewater.

options.text: a solid that fizzes with dilute acid must be a carbonate
options.rationale: Fizzing is the memorable part of the demonstration and feels like the whole result.

mcqs.stem: The gas from a carbonate and dilute acid is bubbled through limewater, which turns milky. What causes the milkiness?

options.text: carbon dioxide gas dissolves and clouds the solution
options.rationale: The gas visibly disappears into the liquid, so dissolving is the intuitive explanation.

options.text: insoluble calcium carbonate forms as a fine white solid
options.rationale: Carbon dioxide reacts with the calcium hydroxide in limewater to precipitate calcium carbonate.

options.text: hydrogen is released and forms bubbles in the liquid
options.rationale: Students who expect hydrogen from acid then explain the cloudiness as trapped bubbles.

options.text: the limewater is neutralised and a sodium salt appears
options.rationale: Students who believe limewater is sodium hydroxide predict a sodium product.

mcqs.stem: A solid fizzes when dilute acid is added. What must be done to confirm that the gas produced is carbon dioxide?

options.text: nothing more; fizzing with acid already shows carbon dioxide
options.rationale: The fizzing is treated as the whole test rather than as the first half of it.

options.text: hold a lighted splint at the mouth of the tube and listen
options.rationale: This is the hydrogen test, chosen by students expecting hydrogen from an acid.

options.text: bubble the gas through limewater and see if it turns milky
options.rationale: Carbon dioxide can be identified with limewater, which turns milky.

options.text: add sodium hydroxide solution and look for a white solid
options.rationale: Students who confuse limewater with sodium hydroxide solution use the wrong alkali.

mcqs.stem: Silver nitrate solution and dilute nitric acid are added to potassium bromide solution. What is seen?

options.text: a yellow precipitate of silver bromide forms
options.rationale: Cream and yellow are close colours and the bromide and iodide labels are easily swapped.

options.text: a white precipitate of silver bromide forms
options.rationale: Silver chloride is demonstrated first and is white, so white becomes the default answer.

options.text: no precipitate forms as silver bromide is soluble
options.rationale: Students who recall that most nitrates and potassium salts are soluble apply that rule too widely.

options.text: a cream precipitate of silver bromide forms
options.rationale: Silver bromide is cream, so a cream precipitate identifies the bromide ion.

mcqs.stem: Why is dilute nitric acid, rather than dilute hydrochloric acid, used in the test for halide ions?

options.text: hydrochloric acid adds chloride ions and gives a false result
options.rationale: Chloride ions from the acid would themselves precipitate white silver chloride from any sample.

options.text: hydrochloric acid is too weak to remove the interfering ions
options.rationale: Students who default to hydrochloric acid explain the choice by strength rather than by ions added.

options.text: nitric acid dissolves the silver nitrate before it is added
options.rationale: Attributing a dissolving role to the acid is a common guess when its purpose is not understood.

options.text: nitric acid makes the precipitate colours easier to see
options.rationale: With no visible effect of its own, the acid is assumed to help with the colours being observed.

mcqs.stem: Which pair of reagents is used to test a solution for sulfate ions?

options.text: barium chloride solution and dilute sulfuric acid
options.rationale: The acid's name matches the ion being tested for, which feels like a helpful pairing.

options.text: barium chloride solution and dilute hydrochloric acid
options.rationale: Sulfate ions produce a white precipitate with barium chloride in the presence of dilute hydrochloric acid.

options.text: silver nitrate solution and dilute nitric acid
options.rationale: The two precipitation tests are learned together and their reagents are readily interchanged.

options.text: sodium hydroxide solution and dilute nitric acid
options.rationale: Sodium hydroxide is the most-used reagent in this topic, so it is picked when the test is not recalled.

mcqs.stem: Why must dilute sulfuric acid never be used in place of dilute hydrochloric acid in the barium chloride test?

options.text: it reacts with barium chloride to give a coloured solution
options.rationale: Students who see no problem with sulfuric acid invent a different, visible reason to reject it.

options.text: it would make the barium sulfate precipitate look yellow
options.rationale: The acid is assumed to affect the colour of the precipitate rather than the ions present.

options.text: it contains sulfate ions, so a precipitate always forms
options.rationale: The acid would supply the very ion being tested for, giving a positive result with every sample.

options.text: it is too concentrated to be handled safely in a test tube
options.rationale: Sulfuric acid's reputation as dangerous makes a safety explanation superficially attractive.

mcqs.stem: A solution gives a white precipitate with barium chloride and dilute hydrochloric acid, and a white precipitate with sodium hydroxide solution that does not dissolve in excess. Which compound could it be?

options.text: magnesium chloride, MgCl2
options.rationale: Students who treat any white precipitate as proof of sulfate do not check which reagent produced it.

options.text: aluminium sulfate, Al2(SO4)3
options.rationale: The sulfate part fits, but only a student who ignores the excess result keeps aluminium.

options.text: calcium chloride, CaCl2
options.rationale: Calcium fits the hydroxide evidence, but a chloride would give no precipitate with barium chloride.

options.text: magnesium sulfate, MgSO4
options.rationale: The sulfate ion gives the barium chloride result and the magnesium ion gives a white hydroxide that does not dissolve in excess.

mcqs.stem: In Required practical 7 a student finds that an unknown compound gives a yellow flame. Why can the compound not yet be named?

options.text: the negative ion in the compound has not been identified
options.rationale: The practical requires the ions in the compound to be identified, and a compound contains both a cation and an anion.

options.text: it can be named; a yellow flame shows it is sodium chloride
options.rationale: The first positive result feels conclusive, and sodium chloride is the sodium compound students know best.

options.text: the flame test shows the compound, not which ion is present
options.rationale: Students who think in substances rather than ions misread what the flame test delivers.

options.text: flame tests are unreliable, so the result must be repeated
options.rationale: Repeating for reliability is a familiar practical instruction and is applied here out of habit.

mcqs.stem: An unknown white solid gives a lilac flame, and its solution gives a cream precipitate with silver nitrate and dilute nitric acid. What is the compound?

options.text: potassium iodide, KI
options.rationale: Students who swap the cream and yellow labels read a cream precipitate as iodide.

options.text: potassium bromide, KBr
options.rationale: A lilac flame identifies potassium and a cream silver halide precipitate identifies bromide.

options.text: lithium bromide, LiBr
options.rationale: Students who swap the Group 1 flame colours read lilac as lithium.

options.text: potassium chloride, KCl
options.rationale: Students who expect all silver halides to look alike do not use the precipitate colour.

mcqs.stem: Instrumental methods are described as accurate, sensitive and rapid. What does sensitive mean here?

options.text: the method is easy to use and needs little training
options.rationale: Automation is associated with convenience, so sensitive is read as user-friendly.

options.text: the equipment breaks easily and must be handled gently
options.rationale: The everyday sense of sensitive as delicate is transferred directly to the apparatus.

options.text: very small amounts of a substance can be detected
options.rationale: Sensitivity is the ability to detect a substance present in a very small amount.

options.text: the method gives the same answer as a chemical test
options.rationale: Students who trust chemical tests most treat agreement with them as the mark of a good method.

mcqs.stem: Which of these is an advantage of instrumental methods compared with the chemical tests in this specification?

options.text: they cost less to buy and need no special training
options.rationale: Machines are assumed to save money and effort, which is the opposite of the truth here.

options.text: they are faster but less accurate than chemical tests
options.rationale: Students who trust their own observations concede speed but not accuracy to instruments.

options.text: they change the sample into a pure form before testing
options.rationale: Purification is associated with careful analysis, so it sounds like a technical advantage.

options.text: they can detect ions present in very small amounts
options.rationale: Instrumental methods are sensitive, so they detect quantities far too small for a chemical test.

mcqs.stem: What happens to the sample in flame emission spectroscopy?

options.text: it is put into a flame and the light given out is analysed
options.rationale: The sample is put into a flame and the light given out is passed through a spectroscope.

options.text: it is heated while light is shone through it and measured
options.rationale: Absorption instruments work this way, and students expect a machine to shine light at a sample.

options.text: it is burned and the mass of the residue left is measured
options.rationale: Burning and weighing is a familiar quantitative technique and is substituted for the unfamiliar one.

options.text: it is put into a flame and the colour is matched by eye
options.rationale: The word flame in the name makes the method look like a more careful flame test.

mcqs.stem: What information can be obtained from the line spectrum produced by flame emission spectroscopy?

options.text: which metal ions are present, but not how much of each
options.rationale: The method grows out of the purely qualitative flame test, so it is assumed to be qualitative too.

options.text: which metal ions are present and their concentrations
options.rationale: The line spectrum can be analysed to identify the metal ions in the solution and measure their concentrations.

options.text: the full range of colours the sample gives out in a flame
options.rationale: The continuous spectrum of white light is the image students already hold of a spectrum.

options.text: which non-metal ions are present and their concentrations
options.rationale: Students who have not fixed that the method analyses metal ions transfer it to the anion tests.

mcqs.stem: A solution's line spectrum contains every line of the calcium reference spectrum, plus several extra lines. What can be concluded?

options.text: calcium is absent because the spectra do not match exactly
options.rationale: Matching is treated as all-or-nothing, as in matching a fingerprint.

options.text: calcium is present, but its concentration cannot be found
options.rationale: Students who see the method as qualitative accept the identification but refuse the measurement.

options.text: calcium is present, together with at least one other metal
options.rationale: A mixture gives the combined line patterns of all the metal ions present in the solution.

options.text: the extra lines are faults in the instrument and are ignored
options.rationale: Unexpected data is often dismissed as instrument error rather than read as evidence.

mcqs.stem: How is the concentration of a metal ion in a solution found using flame emission spectroscopy?

options.text: it cannot be found; the method only names the metals
options.rationale: The flame test origin of the method leads students to assume it is qualitative only.

options.text: by counting the extra lines the sample spectrum shows
options.rationale: Extra lines are misread as a measure of quantity rather than as evidence of other metals.

options.text: by timing how long the flame keeps its colour
options.rationale: Duration is an intuitive but wrong proxy for how much of a substance is present.

options.text: by analysing its line spectrum against a reference set
options.rationale: The line spectrum is analysed, and results are interpreted by comparison with a reference set in the same form.
